sentences: The faction's ascendancy lasted exactly as long as the leader who had assembled it.
Rome's ascendancy over the Mediterranean began with a navy it had to invent from a wrecked ship.
Investigators could not ascertain whether the fire began in the kitchen or the wiring above it.
Before arguing about the cause, ascertain that the thing actually happened.

ascetic.definition: severely self-denying, especially for spiritual reasons
sentences: His ascetic routine allowed one meal, one hour of talk, and no exceptions for holidays.
Ascetic monks slept on stone to keep the body from voting in the soul's decisions.

ascribe.definition: to attribute a cause or origin to
sentences: Never ascribe to malice what is adequately explained by a spreadsheet error.
Historians ascribe the collapse to drought; the survivors ascribed it to their neighbors.
Aseptic technique cut surgical deaths faster than any new instrument ever did.
His prose is aseptic: clean, safe, and entirely free of anything living.
The committee looked askance at a budget that balanced only in the final column.
To look askance is literally to look sideways, which is what suspicion does to a face.
He corrected the intern with an asperity the mistake did not deserve.
Asperity shares a root with "rough": the word is sandpaper for the voice.

aspersion.definition: a damaging or false remark about someone
sentences: He cast aspersions on her research without once naming a paper or a page.
Casting aspersions is cheap; retracting them requires a lawyer.

aspersions.definition: damaging or false remarks about someone
sentences: The letter was three pages of aspersions and one paragraph of verifiable fact.
Aspersions travel faster than corrections and never share a route home.

assail.definition: to attack violently, physically or verbally
sentences: Critics assailed the plan for a week before anyone read past its summary.
Doubts assailed her at three in the morning, which is when doubts do their best work.

assay.definition: to test or analyze the quality of
sentences: The mint assays every bar, since gold is the one metal people bother to fake well.
He assayed the mood of the room and quietly folded his prepared speech.
Royal assent turns a bill into law and has not been refused since 1708.
Her nod was the only assent the motion received, and it carried.

assert.definition: to state firmly; to insist upon a right
sentences: To assert a claim is easy; the burden begins with the next sentence.
She asserted herself for the first time in the meeting and the agenda changed.

assertive.definition: confident and forceful in stating one's position
sentences: Assertive is what we call it when we approve; aggressive is the same behavior we don't.
One assertive question from the audience unraveled forty slides of confidence.

assiduous.definition: showing great care and persistent effort
sentences: Assiduous note-taking saved the project when the only server failed.
The root means "sitting down to it" — assiduity is mostly refusing to get up.
He assiduously avoided the one colleague who might have corrected him.
She worked assiduously for six years and became an overnight success.
It takes a week to read the manual and a year to assimilate it.
The empire assimilated the gods of every province, which made its temples very crowded.

assuage.definition: to soothe or make less intense
sentences: A public apology assuaged nobody, since the private conduct continued unchanged.
Ice cream assuages grief for about eleven minutes, which is still eleven minutes.
To general astonishment, the unknown candidate carried three districts.
His astonishment lasted a second; his recalculation of everything took a month.

astringent.definition: sharp or severe; causing tissue to contract
sentences: Her astringent review of the draft removed both flattery and forty pages.
Unripe persimmons are astringent enough to make the mouth feel upholstered.

astute.definition: shrewd and quick to see advantage
sentences: An astute buyer noticed the roofline sagging and left before the tour ended.
She was astute about people and hopeless about deadlines, a common combination.
What the treaty joined, three bad harvests tore asunder.
The word survives almost entirely inside wedding vows and dramatic weather reports.

atavism.definition: the reappearance of an ancestral trait
sentences: The whale calf born with hind limbs is an atavism, an old blueprint briefly resurfacing.
Mob violence, he argued, is atavism: the crowd remembering something the individual forgot.

attenuate.definition: to weaken or reduce in force
sentences: Distance attenuates the signal until static wins the argument.
Vaccines use attenuated virus: the enemy, sent in weak enough to be studied safely.

attitude.definition: a settled way of thinking or feeling
sentences: His attitude toward deadlines was less defiance than serene disbelief.
Attitude also means an aircraft's angle: both senses describe how something is leaning.

attribute.definition: a quality or characteristic of something
sentences: Patience is the attribute every job listing wants and no interview can test.
In paintings, saints carry attributes — a wheel, a lion — so illiterate viewers could name them.

attuned.definition: receptive to or in harmony with
sentences: Attuned to the room's mood, she cut the presentation in half and won the vote.
Sailors grow attuned to the sound of rigging the way parents do to breathing.
The audacious plan required six strangers to be punctual, which is why it failed.
Audacious enough to ask for the raise in writing, twice, with a chart.
He had the audacity to bill the client for the apology letter.
Audacity swings both ways: the same word praises the explorer and condemns the gatecrasher.

augment.definition: to make greater by adding to
sentences: She augmented her salary by teaching two evening classes she came to prefer.
The choir augmented by twenty voices sounded, to everyone's surprise, quieter.

augury.definition: a sign of what will happen; an omen
sentences: Roman generals delayed battles when the sacred chickens refused to eat — a bad augury.
Empty seats at the premiere were an augury the producers chose to ignore.

august.definition: inspiring respect through dignity and grandeur
sentences: The august hall had hosted four coronations and one very awkward wedding.
An august body of scholars can still be wrong, only more slowly and in better clothing.
The dig proceeded under the auspices of a museum that never sent anyone to see it.
Auspices began as bird-watching for omens; now it means whose logo is on the banner.
Snow on opening night was, the superstitious cast insisted, auspicious.
The launch had an auspicious start and a very expensive middle.
The austere chapel contained one window, one bench, and no explanation.
His austere manner softened exactly once a year, in the presence of his dog.
The authoritarian coach won titles and lost every player who could afford to leave.
Authoritarian regimes rarely announce themselves; they arrive as emergency measures.
Her autocratic editing improved the book and ended the friendship.
The committee was democratic in structure and autocratic in practice.

automate.definition: to make a process operate by machine
sentences: They automated the reporting and discovered nobody had ever read the reports.
Automating a broken process gets you the same mistakes at a much higher speed.
The region became autonomous in name while its budget stayed in the capital.
An autonomous vehicle is only as autonomous as its worst-mapped intersection.
Doctors defend patient autonomy even when the patient chooses badly.
The department traded autonomy for funding and spent a decade regretting the exchange.
The auxiliary generator ran for nine hours and saved the entire experiment.
"Have" and "will" are auxiliary verbs: they carry no meaning, only other verbs.
Avarice is the only deadly sin that improves your credit score.
Dante placed the avaricious face-down, since they had spent life looking at the ground.
The avaricious landlord raised rents twice in a year and wondered why the building emptied.
He was avaricious about money and oddly generous with time.
She averred under oath that the meeting never happened; the parking records disagreed.
To aver is to stake your credit on it, which is why the word appears in court.
His aversion to meetings was strong enough to make him unusually productive.
One bad oyster can install a lifelong aversion in a single evening.

avert.definition: to prevent, or to turn away
sentences: A single phone call averted a strike that had been fifteen months in the making.
She averted her eyes from the screen, which did nothing about the numbers on it.
An avid reader, he owned four thousand books and had shelves for perhaps six hundred.
The word shares a root with avarice: an avid fan is greedy for more.

avocation.definition: a hobby pursued alongside one's job
sentences: Beekeeping was his avocation until the honey outsold his consulting.
Vocation calls you; avocation calls you away, which is the whole difference.

avow.definition: to declare openly and without shame
sentences: He avowed his change of mind in print, which cost him two friends and gained three.
To avow is to own it publicly; to disavow is to hope nobody kept the receipt.

avuncular.definition: kindly and tolerant, like an uncle
sentences: His avuncular advice was warm, confident, and almost entirely wrong.
The anchor's avuncular delivery made even the market crash sound survivable.

axiom.definition: a principle accepted as self-evidently true
sentences: Geometry begins with five axioms; two thousand years of doubt fell on the fifth.
"Follow the money" is treated as an axiom by every reporter under forty.
It is axiomatic in the trade that the last ten percent takes half the time.
What seems axiomatic in one century becomes a research question in the next.
She badgered the office for six weeks until the permit simply appeared.
The verb comes from baiting the animal: relentless, and enjoyed by the wrong party.
An hour of badinage passed before either negotiator mentioned a number.
Their badinage was affectionate and, to everyone else at the table, incomprehensible.
The cat fixed the new sofa with a baleful stare and made its plans.
A baleful glance is not merely unfriendly; it is a forecast.

balk.definition: to hesitate or refuse to proceed
sentences: He balked at the price, then paid it two days later without comment.
The horse balked at the ditch, and the rider continued alone, briefly airborne.
Costs ballooned from a modest estimate to a number nobody would say aloud.
The two-page memo ballooned into a policy, then a department.
The speech was banal enough to be applauded by people who disagreed with it.
Evil, Arendt argued, is often banal: a clerk, a form, a routine afternoon.
The condolence card offered three banalities and one sentence that actually helped.
Banality is what remains after everyone has agreed not to say anything risky.

bandy.definition: to exchange words or pass around casually
sentences: Names were bandied about the newsroom hours before anyone confirmed a single one.
Do not bandy statistics with someone who has read the appendix.

bane.definition: a cause of ruin or persistent misery
sentences: Damp was the bane of the archive, defeating three generations of librarians.
Wolfsbane and henbane are named honestly: the suffix once meant "killer."

banish.definition: to send away permanently; to drive out
sentences: Dante was banished from Florence and spent his exile assigning its citizens to hell.
One good night's sleep banished a fear that had survived a week of argument.
The banter stopped the moment the client walked in, which told him everything.
Their banter had rules older than the friendship itself.
The tax scheme was baroque enough to require its own flowchart and two lawyers.
Baroque originally described a misshapen pearl — an insult that became a period.
A barrage of questions met the announcement, and none of them were friendly.
The artillery barrage lasted a week; the ground never recovered its shape.

barren.definition: unable to produce; bleak and empty
sentences: The barren season yielded one paper, and even that one was mostly footnotes.
The soil looked barren until someone tested it and found the problem was salt.
He acted from base motives and a genuinely good instinct, which confused everyone.
Base metals corrode; noble metals do not — the moral vocabulary came from chemistry.

bastardization.definition: a corrupted or debased version of something
sentences: Purists called the adaptation a bastardization; audiences called it Tuesday.
Every bastardization begins as a shortcut somebody was in a hurry to justify.
The crowd waited with bated breath, which is breathing held back, not baited.
He bated his criticism only after learning the author was in the room.

bauble.definition: a showy trinket of little value
sentences: The medal was a bauble, and he wore it every day for thirty years.
A shop full of baubles will still outsell one honest, expensive thing.
Chaucer is bawdy in a way school editions quietly translate into fog.
The toast started bawdy and ended, unexpectedly, in tears.
The press was baying for a resignation before the facts had finished arriving.
Hounds baying in the valley meant the hunt had turned toward the river.

beatific.definition: showing radiant blessedness or serene joy
sentences: She wore a beatific smile through an hour of criticism, which unsettled the panel.
The infant's beatific expression usually indicates digestion rather than grace.

becoming.definition: flattering or appropriate to the person
sentences: Modesty was becoming in a champion and irritating in a candidate.
The color was becoming; the price was not.
The announcement produced bedlam: three microphones, forty questions, no answers.
Bedlam was a real asylum in London, whose name the city turned into a synonym.

befuddled.definition: confused and unable to think clearly
sentences: Befuddled by the new forms, applicants queued at the wrong desk for two days.
Six hours of jargon left the jury visibly befuddled and quietly resentful.

beg.definition: to ask earnestly; to evade a question
sentences: To beg the question originally meant assuming what you set out to prove.
He begged for one more week and delivered, remarkably, in four days.

begrudge.definition: to resent someone's possession or success
sentences: Nobody begrudged her the prize; several begrudged the speech that followed.
He begrudged every minute spent on paperwork and cheerfully lost hours to the crossword.
The brochure beguiled them into booking a hotel that no longer had a roof.
She beguiled the afternoon with letters she never intended to send.

behoove.definition: to be necessary or proper for
sentences: It would behoove the committee to read the report before praising it.
The word survives almost exclusively in sentences that are about to deliver a warning.
It behooves anyone signing a lease to read the clause about the roof.
"It behooves you" is how English says "you will regret it otherwise."

belabor.definition: to explain or attack at excessive length
sentences: He belabored the obvious for ten minutes while the actual problem waited.
There is no need to belabor the point once the room has visibly agreed.
The beleaguered mayor answered questions about potholes for the ninth straight week.
Creditors beleaguered the office until the phones were simply unplugged.

belfry.definition: a bell tower or the part housing bells
sentences: The belfry held four bells, three of them cracked, one of them illegal to ring.
"Bats in the belfry" locates madness in the tower, which is where the noise is.

belie.definition: to contradict or give a false impression of
sentences: Her calm voice belied a pulse the paramedics later described as impressive.
The tidy figures belied a warehouse in which nothing could be found.
He belittled the discovery until a rival institution announced the same thing.
Jefferson is credited with coining belittle, and critics belittled him for it.
His bellicose speech was aimed at supporters at home, not the enemy abroad.
Bellicose in meetings, he became remarkably reasonable in writing.
A belligerent passenger delayed the flight by ninety minutes and one arrest.
In law, a belligerent is simply a party at war; in life, it is a party at dinner.

bemoan.definition: to express regret or grief about
sentences: Editors have bemoaned the decline of reading in every decade since printing began.
He bemoaned the traffic he had joined by choosing to drive.
The instructions bemused everyone except the child, who assembled it in eight minutes.
Bemused means puzzled, not amused — a distinction most writers have already lost.
He wore a bemused expression through the entire ceremony honoring him.
The bemused silence lasted until someone finally asked what a "synergy audit" was.
The foundation's beneficent grants rebuilt a library and, incidentally, a reputation.
A beneficent tyrant is still a tyrant with better public relations.

benevolent.definition: kind and wishing to do good
sentences: A benevolent stranger paid the fare and disappeared before anyone could object.
Benevolent means wishing well; beneficent means doing well — intention against delivery.
Every generation calls the previous one benighted and is repaid within thirty years.
The word means overtaken by night, which is a kinder image than the insult it became.
The growth was benign, a word that has never sounded so beautiful.
A benign neglect let the meadow return without a single committee meeting.
She had a mathematical bent that the school's curriculum did its best to hide.
Follow your bent, the advice goes, provided somebody pays for it.

bequeath.definition: to leave property or a legacy to someone
sentences: He bequeathed his library to the town and his debts to his nephew.
Shakespeare bequeathed his wife the second-best bed, and scholars have argued ever since.

berate.definition: to scold angrily and at length
sentences: He berated the crew for a delay caused entirely by his own late arrival.
To berate is to scold with the volume up and the clock ignored.
The epidemic bereaved half the village within a single winter.
War bereaves twice: once at the front, and again at every kitchen table.
The argument was bereft of evidence and remarkably confident about it.
Bereft of his notes, he improvised the lecture and was never as good again.
She beseeched the board for one more term and got three more weeks.
Beseeching works on people; it has never once worked on a deadline.

besiege.definition: to surround and press hard upon
sentences: Reporters besieged the house until the family left by a neighbor's garden.
Troy was besieged for ten years and fell, allegedly, to carpentry.
A single anonymous post besmirched a career built over twenty years.
To besmirch is to smear: the metaphor was mud long before it was media.

besotted.definition: infatuated to the point of foolishness
sentences: Besotted with the prototype, investors ignored the fact that it never worked twice.
He was besotted enough to move countries and sensible enough to keep the lease.

bestow.definition: to confer or give as a gift
sentences: The university bestowed an honorary degree on a donor who had never read a book.
Titles bestowed cheaply are worn loudly.

betoken.definition: to be a sign of; to indicate
sentences: Empty shelves betokened a shortage the government was still denying.
A red sky at night betokens nothing except that people love a rhyme.

betray.definition: to be disloyal; to reveal unintentionally
sentences: His steady voice betrayed nothing; his hands betrayed everything.
The map betrayed the route long before the guide admitted they were lost.

betrothed.definition: the person one is engaged to marry
sentences: Her betrothed arrived two days late and blamed a river that had not flooded.
In the letters he calls her his betrothed, a word already old-fashioned in 1890.

bevy.definition: a large group of people or things
sentences: A bevy of consultants arrived, produced a chart, and left before anything was decided.
The collective noun began with quails and swans and has since escaped into offices.
The sample was biased toward people willing to answer a twenty-minute phone survey.
Everyone can spot a biased referee except the crowd that is winning.
The trail bifurcates at the ridge, and both branches are labeled "summit."
The case bifurcated into a criminal trial and a civil one, each blaming the other's delay.
His bilious column attacked the mayor, the weather, and a passing dog.
Medieval doctors blamed bad temper on bile, and the insult outlived the medicine.

bilk.definition: to cheat someone out of money
sentences: He bilked investors out of millions with a fund that owned one photocopier.
Bilking works best on people too embarrassed to admit they were bilked.

blanch.definition: to turn pale; to briefly scald food
sentences: He blanched at the estimate and asked, hopefully, whether it included tax.
Blanch the almonds and the skins slip off like bad excuses.

bland.definition: lacking flavor, interest, or strong feeling
sentences: The statement was so bland it could have been issued by any of the four parties.
Hospital food is bland by design, which is its only design.
The foul was so blatant that even the home crowd stopped arguing.
Blatant errors survive longest, since everyone assumes someone else has flagged them.
The forecast was bleak, and the second forecast was worse and better documented.
A bleak landscape has its admirers; a bleak balance sheet has none.
Potato blight emptied a country and rewrote the map of two continents.
The empty lot was a blight the council discussed annually for eleven years.
A blighted harvest meant the village ate seed corn and hoped for a mild spring.
His blighted career recovered abruptly when the accusation collapsed.
A blinkered focus on quarterly numbers cost the company its only patent.
Blinkers keep a horse from panicking and a person from noticing.
His blithe assurance that "it'll be fine" preceded every disaster of the trip.
She showed a blithe disregard for rules that had, admittedly, never been explained.

bluster.definition: loud, aggressive talk with little substance
sentences: Behind the bluster was a negotiator who had already accepted the terms.
Bluster is what wind and executives have in common.

boast.definition: to speak with excessive pride; to possess
sentences: The town boasts two museums, one of which is a shed with a plaque.
He boasted about the deal until the details were published.
The bogus certificate hung in the lobby for four years before anyone checked.
Bogus once named a machine for making counterfeit coins, which is a fittingly fake origin.
A boisterous crowd filled the hall and drowned out the string quartet entirely.
Boisterous at nine, silent at ten: the class had discovered the substitute's limits.
New data bolstered a theory that had been surviving on charm alone.
The word is a pillow: to bolster is to prop something up so it does not sag.

bolt.definition: to run away suddenly; to eat hurriedly
sentences: The horse bolted at the umbrella and stopped, sheepishly, four fields later.
He bolted his lunch in ninety seconds and spent the afternoon regretting it.
Strip the bombast from the speech and one modest proposal remains.
Bombast was originally cotton padding — the word means stuffing, and always did.
His bombastic introduction lasted longer than the lecture it introduced.
Bombastic prose is easy to write and impossible to finish reading.
The conference ran on bonhomie, coffee, and a shared dread of the closing plenary.
His bonhomie evaporated the instant the contract was on the table.
The new bridge was a boon to everyone except the ferryman.
Rain in June is a boon; the same rain in August ruins the harvest.
The boor talked through the entire quartet and complained about the acoustics.
Boor once simply meant farmer, which says more about cities than about farmers.
His boorish remarks emptied the table faster than the fire alarm had that morning.
Boorish behavior at a wedding is remembered longer than the vows.
A cube of bouillon rescued a soup that had otherwise given up.
The word shares a root with "boil," which is the entire recipe.

bowdlerize.definition: to censor by removing offensive parts
sentences: The film was bowdlerized for television until the plot no longer made sense.
Thomas Bowdler cleaned up Shakespeare and earned the rare fate of becoming a verb.

brandish.definition: to wave something threateningly or ostentatiously
sentences: He brandished the report like a weapon and never once opened it.
Brandishing an umbrella at a taxi is the most British form of combat.

bravado.definition: a show of courage meant to impress
sentences: The bravado lasted until the first question he could not answer.
Bravado is courage's understudy: same costume, no rehearsal.
The job needed brains and brawn, and the budget covered one of them.
Brawn moved the piano; brains had already measured the doorway.
A brazen forgery signed with the wrong century's spelling fooled two experts anyway.
She made a brazen request and, because nobody expected it, got exactly that.
Brevity is the soul of wit, said a character in a very long speech.
The email's brevity was mistaken for anger, which cost three days of clarification.
She bridled at the suggestion that the discovery had been lucky.
Bridle your enthusiasm long enough to read the contract.
The committee bristled at being called ceremonial, which rather proved the point.
A cat bristles to look larger; people do it to sound larger.

broach.definition: to raise a subject for discussion
sentences: Nobody would broach the topic of the missing funds until the auditor did.
The word means to pierce a barrel: broaching a subject lets the pressure out.

broadside.definition: a forceful attack in speech or writing
sentences: Her broadside against the proposal filled two pages and ended three careers.
A ship's broadside fired every gun at once, which is how the metaphor earned its force.
The speech offered bromides about teamwork to a room that had just been laid off.
Bromide was once a sedative, which explains what the word came to mean.

brooch.definition: an ornamental pin worn on clothing
sentences: The brooch was paste, and the insurance claim was not.
She chose her brooch the way other diplomats chose their words.
The chairman brooked no interruption, which made the meetings short and useless.
She would brook criticism of her methods but never of her data.

browbeat.definition: to bully with words or threats
sentences: He browbeat the junior staff into agreeing and called it consensus.
Browbeating produces compliance and, reliably, a resignation letter six weeks later.
"No," he said brusquely, and turned back to the screen.
She answered brusquely, then spent the afternoon writing an apologetic paragraph.
The small studio bucked the trend and released a two-hour film with no explosions.
The horse bucked, the trend bucked, and both threw somebody off.
The painting's bucolic calm hid the fact that the field had been worked by children.
A bucolic weekend cured him of wanting a bucolic life.
A film buff spotted the continuity error the director's whole crew had missed.
Fire buffs once wore buff-colored coats, which is where the fan got his name.

buffer.definition: something that lessens a shock or conflict
sentences: Savings acted as a buffer between one bad month and total catastrophe.
The neutral state was a buffer, which is a polite word for battlefield.

bullion.definition: gold or silver in bulk form
sentences: The vault held bullion worth more than the building housing it.
Bullion is money that has not yet been asked to be interesting.

bulwark.definition: a defensive wall or strong protection
sentences: A free press is the standard bulwark cited in speeches and cut in budgets.
The dunes were the town's only bulwark against a sea that kept auditioning.
A bumbling attempt at repair turned a leak into an indoor fountain.
The bumbling detective solves the case by tripping over the evidence, which audiences forgive.

buoyant.definition: cheerful and resilient; able to float
sentences: She stayed buoyant through the rejections and kept a folder of them for scale.
Markets described as buoyant have a habit of remembering gravity.
Three signatures were needed, and the bureaucracy required them in an impossible order.
Bureaucracy literally means rule by desk, which anyone who has visited one can confirm.
The side project burgeoned into a company with an office and a legal department.
Burgeon began as a word for buds opening, and it still carries the spring in it.

burnish.definition: to polish; to improve a reputation
sentences: The donation burnished a reputation that three lawsuits had dulled.
He burnished the anecdote with each retelling until it gleamed and was untrue.
He buttressed the argument with three studies, two of which he had not read.
Flying buttresses let cathedral walls become windows, which is architecture's best magic trick.
The word once meant obedient, then cheerful, and only lately what it means now.
The portrait's buxom subject was, the label revealed, the painter's landlady.
The hotel preserved a bygone elegance and, unfortunately, bygone plumbing.
Let bygones be bygones, says the person who wrote everything down.
The approval process was byzantine enough that consultants existed solely to navigate it.
Byzantine court intrigue was so tangled that the empire's name became an adjective for it.
A cabal of three deans reversed a decision the full faculty had spent a year making.
Every committee that meets before the meeting is, technically, a cabal.
The orchestra's tuning is cacophonous by design and the best part of the evening.
Cacophonous debate is still better than a silence somebody enforced.
A cacophony of alarms went off, none of them indicating an actual fire.
The Greek roots mean "bad sound," which is a fair review of most group chats.
Three weeks of exams left him cadaverous and fluent in medieval trade law.
The portrait's cadaverous face was the painter's revenge for an unpaid fee.

cajole.definition: to persuade by flattery or coaxing
sentences: She cajoled the landlord into fixing the boiler with compliments and one small pie.
Cajoling works where demanding fails, which every toddler discovers before age three.
The callous reply to a grieving family was read aloud in court.
Skin grows callous to protect itself, which is exactly what the metaphor means.
A callow recruit argued with the safety officer once and never again.
The word meant featherless: a callow bird cannot yet fly, and neither can he.

calumny.definition: a false statement meant to damage a reputation
sentences: The pamphlet was pure calumny, and it outsold every honest account of the trial.
Calumny needs no evidence, only repetition and a willing audience.

cameo.definition: a brief notable appearance or portrayal
sentences: The author's cameo lasts eleven seconds and is the film's most discussed scene.
The chapter is a cameo of the whole era, cut small and carved deep.

campaign.definition: an organized effort toward a goal
sentences: The campaign to save the theater raised half the money and all of the attention.
Campaign comes from "open field": armies fought there before marketers borrowed the word.

canard.definition: an unfounded rumor or false story
sentences: The canard that the bridge was sinking survived four engineering reports.
Canard is French for duck; the fake story apparently waddles.
Her candid assessment cost her the promotion and earned her the department's trust.
A candid photograph catches you before you can arrange your face.
His candidness in the interview was refreshing until it reached the legal department.
Candidness costs nothing to give and a great deal to receive.
The memo's candor about the failure is why the company survived it.
Candor is honesty without the flattering angle.

canny.definition: shrewd and careful, especially in business
sentences: A canny buyer waited three weeks and got the same house for less.
Canny is astute with its wallet already closed.

canon.definition: an accepted body of works or rules
sentences: Ten novels entered the canon that decade, and eight were by people nobody had published before.
Every argument about the canon is really an argument about who assigns reading.
The canonical version of the experiment omits the three attempts that failed.
Which recipe is canonical depends entirely on whose grandmother is in the room.

canonize.definition: to declare a saint; to treat as authoritative
sentences: Critics canonized the novel so quickly that its flaws became features.
The church canonized her four centuries after burning her records.
The speech was cant: virtue words arranged around a contract award.
Cant also means the private jargon of a trade, which is often the same thing.
The cantankerous neighbor objected to the fence, the color, and the concept of neighbors.
He grew cantankerous with age, having decided politeness had never once helped him.

canto.definition: a major division of a long poem
sentences: The Inferno's first canto gets read in every survey course; the other thirty-three do not.
Each canto ends on a cliff, which is how epic poems kept audiences awake.

capacity.definition: the ability or maximum amount possible
sentences: The hall's capacity is four hundred, and six hundred tickets were somehow sold.
She has the capacity for the work and no appetite for the meetings.
The studio capitulated after nine weeks and restored the original ending.
To capitulate was originally to negotiate terms in chapters — surrender with paperwork.

caprice.definition: a sudden unpredictable change of mind
sentences: The schedule changed on the caprice of a director who had not read it.
Caprice comes from a word for a hedgehog-headed shudder, which is how whims feel.
Funding was capricious, generous one year and invisible the next.
Mountain weather is capricious enough to require three coats and one apology.

captious.definition: eager to find fault over trifles
sentences: The captious reviewer devoted a paragraph to a misplaced comma and none to the argument.
Captious questions are designed to catch, not to learn.
The cardinal rule of the lab was to label everything, and it was broken weekly.
Cardinal comes from "hinge": the things everything else swings on.

careen.definition: to lurch or swerve while moving fast
sentences: The cart careened down the hill and ended its career in a hedge.
The negotiations careened between collapse and celebration twice in one afternoon.

caricature.definition: an exaggerated portrayal for comic effect
sentences: The cartoon was a caricature: one enormous nose and a policy nobody could defend.
Argue against a caricature of a view and you have won nothing at all.
A carping colleague can drain more energy than an outright enemy.
The carping notes in the margin outnumbered the sentences they surrounded.

carrion.definition: the decaying flesh of dead animals
sentences: Vultures find carrion by smell from a mile up, which is a horrifying talent.
The metaphor is unkind but exact: the lawyers circled like birds over carrion.
The cartographer left the interior blank rather than invent rivers, which was rare honesty.
Medieval cartographers filled empty space with monsters; modern ones use logos.

cartography.definition: the art and science of making maps
sentences: Cartography is never neutral: what gets named and centered is an argument.
Satellite imagery finished the geography and left cartography arguing about borders.
The report castigated the agency for delays it had documented in its own memos.
He castigated the team publicly and apologized privately, in that revealing order.
The castigation lasted twenty minutes and taught nothing that two sentences would not have.
Public castigation buys obedience and sells loyalty.
The eruption was a cataclysm that ended a civilization and preserved its bread.
Financial cataclysms are always obvious afterward and unthinkable the week before.
The asteroid's arrival was cataclysmic for dinosaurs and career-making for mammals.
A cataclysmic first act leaves a play nowhere to go.
The strike was not the cause but the catalyst; the grievances were a decade old.
A catalyst speeds the reaction and walks away unchanged, which is enviable.
He issued a categorical denial on Monday and a careful clarification on Friday.
Kant's categorical imperative admits no "unless," which is why it is so hard to live by.
Writing the letter was cathartic; sending it would have been catastrophic.
Greek audiences went to tragedies for a cathartic cry and a clean walk home.
Her taste in music was catholic enough to include both plainsong and speed metal.
Lowercase catholic means all-embracing, which is where the capitalized word got its ambition.

caucus.definition: a closed meeting of a faction
sentences: The caucus met at seven and had decided the vote before the public session opened.
Iowa's caucuses require standing in a corner of a gym, which is democracy at its most literal.
Her caustic aside was quoted for years, usually by people who had not been insulted.
Caustic soda eats through pipes; caustic remarks manage friendships.
His cavalier attitude toward safety ended when the inspector arrived unannounced.
A cavalier answer to a careful question is its own kind of insult.

cease.definition: to stop or bring to an end
sentences: Production ceased in March and resumed, under a new name, in April.
"Cease and desist" says the same thing twice, which lawyers charge for separately.

cede.definition: to give up power or territory formally
sentences: The company ceded the market rather than fight a competitor with deeper pockets.
Nations cede territory on paper long before anyone moves a fence.
The refund arrived with a celerity that suggested somebody feared the press.
Celerity shares a root with accelerate and nothing at all with celery.

censor.definition: to suppress objectionable parts of material
sentences: The letters were censored so heavily that the surviving words formed a haiku.
Censoring a book is the most reliable way to guarantee it is read.
The senate's censure carried no penalty and ended a thirty-year career.
Censure is disapproval with the minutes taken.

centrifuge.definition: a machine spinning to separate substances
sentences: The centrifuge sorts blood into layers that tell a doctor more than the patient can.
Spun long enough in a centrifuge, even loyalty separates by density.
The film is cerebral to a fault: three ideas, no pulse.
His approach was cerebral, hers instinctive, and the argument they had was inevitable.

chaff.definition: worthless material; husks separated from grain
sentences: Separating wheat from chaff is easy with grain and nearly impossible with advice.
The report was ninety pages of chaff around four useful paragraphs.
To his chagrin, the error was on the slide behind him, enlarged and backlit.
Chagrin is embarrassment with a bruise on the pride.

chamber.definition: an enclosed space or legislative body
sentences: The lower chamber passed the bill, and the upper chamber buried it politely.
The burial chamber had been sealed for three thousand years and looted for two thousand nine hundred.

champion.definition: to support or defend a cause vigorously
sentences: She championed the unglamorous reform that saved more lives than any drug that decade.
He championed the idea until it succeeded, then championed his role in it.
The charlatan sold a cure, a certificate, and a follow-up appointment he never kept.
Charlatan comes from an Italian word for chatter — the credential is the talking.
